title: Shabbat with friends of other faiths
word: Shabbat with friends of other faiths
hookLine: sharing a Shabbat table with non-Jewish friends
tomorrow: Isaiah has one word for how Shabbat should feel. which one?

cards: Group chats run on comparisons: is this like that? Noa's friend Hana, from the school play, is coming to Friday dinner.

Hana's family is Muslim, and she texts the obvious question: is Shabbat like jumu'ah, our Friday prayers? Owen is coming too, and he's already asking where he should sit. The honest answer to Hana is yes, and no.
Both halves are worth hearing, and both fit at one table.

teach.h: A SIGN, AND AN OPEN TABLE.
teach.b: Start with the question underneath: who is Shabbat for? The Torah calls it a sign between God and the children of Israel, so it belongs to the Jewish people in a particular way.

teach.h: A HOUSE OF PRAYER FOR ALL PEOPLES.
teach.b: And yet Isaiah pictures foreigners who join themselves to God and keep the Sabbath, and calls God's house "a house of prayer for all peoples." Both stand side by side: a day that's Jewish, at a table that's open.
A guest doesn't have to say the blessings, keep the laws, or know when to stand. Eating, watching, and saying amen if they want to is plenty. Now a neighbor who says it too.
In Islam, Friday is the day of congregation, and the Qur'an, in Pickthall's translation, tells believers to "haste unto remembrance of Allah and leave your trading."

Shared ground: a weekly day when the market stops and people turn to God together. And one honest difference. The very next verse says that when the prayer is over, people may go out into the land and seek God's bounty.

teach.h: AN HOUR, OR A WHOLE DAY.
teach.b: Jumu'ah sets apart a gathering in the middle of the day; Shabbat sets apart the whole day, sunset to sunset, from work.
Two weekly days, set apart in two ways, and a friend from one is welcome at the other's table. Something to tell a friend tonight: Isaiah imagines foreigners keeping the Sabbath.

how: Some Jewish families invite friends of other faiths to Friday-night dinner; guests are welcome to watch the candles, kiddush and the blessing over bread without saying them, and hosts usually explain each step briefly.

games.q: what does “shabbat with friends of other faiths” mean?
o: a Jewish Shabbat table with guests of other faiths
a shared holy day kept by several religions at once
a Shabbat service held at a church or a mosque

games.q: two weekly days — tap the pairs.
p: a sign between God and Israel
a house of prayer for all peoples

s: Isaiah pictures foreigners keeping the Sabbath
Isaiah 56:6-7: those who join themselves to God and keep the Sabbath; a house of prayer for all peoples.
a guest at a Shabbat table is expected to say the blessings
watching, eating, and an amen if they want is plenty.
jumu'ah and Shabbat both rest from work for the whole day
the Qur'an pauses trade for the Friday prayer, then says people may go seek God's bounty. Shabbat rests sunset to sunset.

games.q: your roommate, who is Hindu, is coming to Friday dinner and worries she'll do something wrong. what's the most fitting thing to tell her?
o: just come: guests are welcome to watch, eat, and skip the blessings.
learn the Hebrew blessings first, so you can join in properly.
come for dessert, after the rituals are done, so it's easier.
games.why: Shabbat is a Jewish sign, and the table is open. a guest doesn't have to say or know anything to belong at it.

practice: Bring to mind one friend from a different background who has never seen a Shabbat table, or any table like it in your own life.
Write them a short invitation now: when, what you'll eat, and that they don't need to know or say anything. Send it, or keep it for the right week.

wordCard.voice: Shabbat with friends of other faiths: a day that's Jewish, at a table that's open, where a guest only has to come.

orig.note: Hebrew: a house of prayer for all peoples, from Isaiah 56:7.

carryVoice: For today: a table for everyone, and nobody needs the words to be welcome. Until tomorrow.
